stacks.name: Static HTML
stacks.summary: The reference page with no JavaScript at all. Every interaction is a full page load: forms post and links navigate. It shows what the network and the server cost on their own.

stacks.name: Vanilla JS
stacks.summary: The reference page plus one small, hand-written module: event delegation, fetch and DOM updates, no library. It stands for the least JavaScript these interactions need.

idioms.choice: The module loads in <head> as type=module, so it runs after parsing without blocking it.
Search and category filters hide and show the cards the server rendered; the quick view fetches the product's details as JSON when opened.

stacks.name: Alpine.js
stacks.summary: The reference page with Alpine's directives written into the server's markup. One module, Alpine bundled with the page's stores and components, loads up front and starts Alpine over the server-rendered HTML; stores hold the cart and the filters, and the cart, the quick view and the newsletter call the shared JSON API.

idioms.choice: Alpine is installed from npm and imported into the page's bundle ("As a module", which the installation guide calls the more robust approach) rather than loaded as the script-tag build: the page has its own stores and components, and its code imports the scenario's helpers, so it needs a build step anyway. Everything is registered between importing Alpine and the single Alpine.start() call, as the guide requires, and window.Alpine is set as in the guide's snippet.

Alpine leaves the bundler open. Vite bundles and minifies Alpine with the page's code into one module, and the Node server writes its <script type="module"> tag into <head> from Vite's manifest, as Vite's backend integration describes. A module script is deferred, like the defer attribute that the script-tag installation asks for.

Vite's modulepreload polyfill is turned off (build.modulePreload.polyfill: false), the alternative the backend integration guide gives to importing it: the build is one chunk, and the page has no <link rel="modulepreload"> for it to handle.

The page is the app's own server template (page.js), rendered per request by the scenario's small Node page server, which also takes the form posts made without JavaScript. It copies the reference markup, ids and text, and writes Alpine's directives into it. The reference render has no attribute hooks on the product cards (x-show), the result count and the newsletter status (x-text) or the dialog's contents, so the app does not use it.

The cart and the filters, which several parts of the page share, are global stores (Alpine.store) registered from the bundle before Alpine.start(). They start from JSON that the server renders into the page (the cart it read from the cookie, the category, and the products it rendered a card for), so every binding starts on the text the server rendered.

Parts of the page that only read or change store state (the header's cart line, the search form, the category links, the result count and the product list) are data-less components, each with a bare x-data, rather than one component around the whole page.

The newsletter form and the quick view dialog are components registered with Alpine.data from the bundle. The server passes their starting state as initial parameters (x-data="newsletter(...)"), written as JSON and escaped for the attribute.

Search and category filters run in the browser over the cards the server rendered, like the docs' search input: the search box is bound to the filters store with x-model, each card has x-show, and the result count is a getter. Nothing is fetched, so there is no debounce and results change on every key.

The search box uses x-model.fill, so the query starts from the box's value: the one the server rendered, or what someone typed before the script arrived, which plain x-model would overwrite with the store's value.

Cards that the server filters out carry style="display: none" instead of the reference's hidden attribute, because x-show hides and shows with the inline display property and leaves the attribute alone.

No x-cloak: the server renders every element in the state that Alpine starts from, so nothing flickers while Alpine loads. x-cloak would also need an [x-cloak] rule, which the shared stylesheet does not have.
Forms and links keep their action and href, so the page works without JavaScript and before Alpine starts; Alpine takes them over with @submit.prevent and @click.prevent.
Add to cart, the quick view and the newsletter call the shared JSON API with fetch, from async store and component methods.

A card's Quick view link dispatches a quick-view event with $dispatch; the dialog component listens with @quick-view.window, fetches the product, sets it for its x-text bindings and opens with showModal(). It opens right after the product is set, without $nextTick: Alpine applies the bindings in a microtask, before the next frame is painted, so the dialog never shows the previous product.
The newsletter component reads the address through x-ref when the form is sent, rather than binding it with x-model, since nothing else needs it.

stacks.name: Astro + Preact
stacks.summary: Astro renders the page on demand with its Node adapter. The header, the catalog, the quick view and the newsletter are Preact islands, each hydrated when it is needed; they share state through nanostores and call Astro Actions, which the same forms also use without JavaScript.

idioms.choice: output: 'server': the page is rendered on demand for every request, since its header reads the cart cookie. HTML streaming stays on, the default.
The Node adapter in standalone mode. The start command runs its built server, node ./dist/server/entry.mjs, which reads HOST and PORT and also serves the built client files.

Astro components render everything static (the document, the header's brand, the introduction, the footer) with no JavaScript. Four Preact islands hold the interactive parts: the cart summary, the catalog, the quick view and the newsletter.

The cart summary and the catalog (search, categories, result count and cards, one island because they share the filters) hydrate with client:load: they are on the first screen and must respond at once.
The quick view dialog hydrates with client:idle: it is closed until someone asks for it, and a request made before it hydrates waits in its store.
The newsletter, below the 50 cards, hydrates with client:visible. Until then its form still posts without JavaScript.

Islands share state through nanostores and @nanostores/preact: $cart (set by add to cart, read by the header) and $quickView (set by the catalog, read by the dialog). Only the browser writes to the stores; server renders use props.
The page reads the cart cookie and the URL on the server and passes islands their data as props: the cart summary, and the 50 products without descriptions for the catalog.

Search and category filters run in the browser, in the catalog island's state, over the products it received as props: results change on every key without a request, so there is no debounce. The island already holds the listing, so asking the server on each key would only add a request and the scenario's 200 ms wait. Without JavaScript, the GET form and the category links render the filtered page on the server, as in the reference.

Astro Actions instead of the shared JSON API: addToCart and newsletter accept form data, getProduct takes JSON for the quick view, and the islands call them through the actions client. The cart cookie is written with context.cookies in the scenario's format.

The forms work without JavaScript: method=post, with the action's query string (?_action=…) as their action, so the server runs the same action and renders the page. Once hydrated, the islands call the action instead of submitting.
An add to cart posted without JavaScript redirects (303) back to the page it came from on success, so reloading does not add the item again (POST/Redirect/GET).
A newsletter form posted without JavaScript is answered with the page rendered from the action's result, Astro's default for form actions.
The newsletter action validates the address with Zod, using the scenario's rule and message, and both the page and the island show that field's message with isInputError().

security.allowedDomains trusts the proxy's X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host for https://localhost on any port, so Astro.url is the address the browser uses and the origin check on form posts and actions, on by default, stays on.

Scenario rule: /assets/app.css is linked with a plain <link> in the layout's <head>, the documented way to load a static stylesheet, with no component styles or CSS imports. Astro adds only its 62-byte inline style for <astro-island>.

Scenario rule: card and dialog images are plain elements, the framework's own image syntax inside Preact components, with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding. Astro's would re-encode the shared images and cannot be used inside framework components.
Defaults kept: no <ClientRouter /> and no prefetching, both opt-in. The site is one page, and its filters run in place.

stacks.name: CycleWire
stacks.summary: The reference page activated by CycleWire, built from this repository's source, so every run measures the commit it runs on: the core loads up front, and each interaction's code loads when someone reaches for it. Nothing hydrates.

idioms.choice: The core loads as a module in <head>, with a modulepreload link, as the performance guide recommends.
Vite bundles the page's script, and fromGlob(import.meta.glob('./actions/*.js')) registers every action as its own chunk. Vite preloads a chunk's dependencies when it is imported.

The server writes the entry's <script> and <link rel="modulepreload"> tags from Vite's manifest, and the modulepreload polyfill is turned off rather than imported, as the backend integration guide allows. Preloading an action's imports stays on.

Add to cart, the action most visitors use first, is preloaded with the page: the server writes <link rel="modulepreload"> for its chunk and the chunks it imports, from Vite's manifest, so a tap on it right after the page appears waits only for the server. Everything else loads on intent, the default, and on touch screens also once the page is idle.
The cart header is bound to a store the server serializes (cw-store, cw-bind); cyclewire/signals arrives with the cart action.
The quick view fetches JSON and renders it with cyclewire/dom, which arrives with that action.
The quick view link names its data with cw-prefetch, and the prefetch plugin fetches it on intent, next to the action's code; the action's ctx.fetch() takes that response.

stacks.name: htmx
stacks.summary: The reference page from a plain Node server, with htmx attributes on its links and forms. Without JavaScript they load full pages; with htmx they fetch HTML fragments (the results, the quick view, the cart header, the newsletter message) and swap them in.

idioms.choice: htmx.min.js loads with a plain <script> in <head>, as the installation guide describes. The guide mentions neither defer nor the ESM build for a script tag, so neither is used.

No build step: the app's server serves dist/htmx.min.js from the htmx.org npm package at a content-hashed URL. The guide needs no build system and leaves serving the npm file to the app's own tooling.
A plain node:http server, no web framework: a hypermedia app can use any server-side technology.

Progressive enhancement: each hx-get or hx-post repeats its link's href or its form's action (the docs' other option, hx-boost, swaps the whole body), and the server checks the HX-Request header to answer with a fragment or with the full page.

Answers that depend on HX-Request carry Vary: HX-Request, and htmx.config.historyRestoreAsHxRequest is off (set in a <meta name="htmx-config"> tag), as the caching section requires when HX-Request selects fragments.
htmx.config.reportValidityOfForms is on, which the validation section says to always do, so an invalid field is reported as a native form submission would.

Search follows the Active Search example, with the trigger on the search form so the query goes with the form's category field and Enter searches at once: hx-trigger="submit, input changed delay:200ms". The delay is the scenario's 200 ms; the example uses 500 ms. Only the results are swapped, never the input, and no history entry is pushed, as in the example.
Search and category requests both fill #products and share hx-sync="#products:replace", so a newer one aborts one still in flight. The hx-sync page recommends replace for active search.

Answers that update more than their target carry <hx-partial> swap commands, added in 2.0.11 for responses that update several parts of the page (its example is #cart-count and #cart-total): the result count, the cart header, and after a category link the search form and the category links.
Add to cart is answered with partials only, so the form that posted is left unchanged without hx-swap="none".
The docs' first choice for updating other content is to expand the target, but the reference markup has no element around the result count and the list, so the count is a partial.

Quick view swaps the product into the <dialog> and opens it as a modal with hx-on::after-swap="if (!this.open) this.showModal()": htmx has no dialog attribute, and hx-on is its way to handle an htmx event inline.
Forms sent by htmx get their fragment back directly, without the Post/Redirect/Get that the plain forms keep.
An invalid newsletter address is answered with 200 and the message, which htmx swaps by default, rather than 422 plus a responseHandling rule, the alternative the docs show.

stacks.name: Next.js
stacks.summary: App Router Server Components render the page per request from the URL and the cart cookie. Server Actions add to the cart and sign up for the newsletter, typing in the search box updates ?q= for the server to render the results, and the quick view is an intercepted route shown in a modal.

idioms.choice: Built with next build (Turbopack, the default bundler) and served by next start, the Node.js server of the deployment docs. --hostname 127.0.0.1 binds it to the loopback address; the port comes from $PORT, which next start reads.

turbopack.root is bench/, the documented setting when a project imports files from outside its folder: the app imports the shared catalog, cart and markup modules from bench/scenario/. Next.js uses the same root for output file tracing.

Every request renders on the server (dynamic rendering, the default for request-time APIs): the root layout reads the cart cookie with cookies() and the page filters by its searchParams. Cache Components, opt-in in Next.js 16, is not enabled.
The header with the cart is in the root layout, the UI every page shares. Layouts do not render again on navigation, so a filter or a search fetches only the page.

Add to cart is a Server Action passed to <form action> in a Server Component, so the form posts before hydration and without JavaScript, and the server answers with the page. The product id is a hidden input, the reference's markup and the forms guide's alternative to bind().

The action sets the cart cookie with cookies().set(). Setting a cookie makes Next.js render the current route again and send it in the action's response, so it calls neither refresh() nor revalidatePath().

The newsletter form is a Client Component with useActionState and a Server Action that returns the message, as the forms guide shows for messages from the server; before hydration the form posts and the page comes back with the message. The button is disabled while the action is pending, as in the guide.

Live search as the Next.js Learn course teaches it: the query is in the URL, useDebouncedCallback (use-debounce) calls router.replace(), and the page's Server Components render the results. The course waits 300 ms; the scenario sets 200 ms for every stack that searches on the server. The course's Suspense boundary and skeleton around the results are left out (see loading.js below).

The page passes the query and category it read from searchParams to the search box as props, where the course's box reads useSearchParams(): the results are data the page loads, and while the quick view is open the URL is /products/<id> but the list behind it keeps its query. The box follows navigations it did not make, so choosing a category clears it.
The search form is next/form: Enter navigates on the client, and without JavaScript it is a GET form that keeps the selected category in a hidden field.

Category filters are <Link>s to /?category=…, and every link keeps the default prefetching. The routes are dynamic and have no loading.js, so, as the prefetching guide describes, the prefetches of links in view carry no page data, and the page is rendered on click.

No loading.js, although the navigation docs suggest one for dynamic routes. With it, every full page load sends the page behind the loading fallback and reveals it with an inline script, so without JavaScript only the fallback shows, and the first product images, the page's LCP element, would sit inside the boundary. The streaming guide advises keeping LCP elements outside Suspense boundaries and not adding boundaries you don't need; the catalog renders from memory in one pass.

The quick view uses the docs' pattern for modals: an @modal parallel route with the intercepting route (.)products/[id]. A Quick view link to /products/<id> opens the product in a modal over the list, with its own URL; back closes it and forward reopens it. On a full page load, /products/<id> renders the shop with the dialog open, which is how the reference shows a quick view without JavaScript, and @modal/page.js renders nothing, so a navigation to / closes that one.

The modal is a native <dialog id="quick-view"> opened with showModal() in an effect, as in the docs' nextgram example. Its Close button (a method="dialog" form) and Escape close it, and the close event calls router.back().

Scenario-forced: the stylesheet is a plain <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.css"> in the root layout's <head>, not an imported CSS file (the docs' default); the docs note that React's <link rel="stylesheet"> can be used. React adds a preload for it.

Scenario-forced: product images are plain elements with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding, not next/image, which serves resized copies from its image optimizer. React preloads the four eager ones.

stacks.name: Qwik City
stacks.summary: The page as a Qwik City app on its Node.js server adapter: rendered per request and resumed in the browser, nothing hydrates. Route loaders read the cart cookie and the URL, the forms are route actions, search and filters are signals, and the quick view fetches its product through server$.

idioms.choice: The production server is the one `npm run qwik add node-server` sets up: Node's http.createServer with Qwik City's Node middleware, which renders the page and serves the client build from dist/. It starts with `npm run serve`. The adapter's entry listens on $PORT; it also takes $HOST (127.0.0.1), which the template leaves out.
`npm run build` runs `qwik build`: the client build, the adapter's server build and a type check. The adapter's static generation step prerenders no page, since none is listed for it.
The page is rendered for every request and sets no cacheControl, as the docs advise for pages that differ per visitor: the header shows the visitor's cart.
The Node middleware takes the site's origin from the ORIGIN environment variable (the runner sets it to the proxy's address), and its CSRF check compares form posts' Origin header with it.

Code loading keeps Qwik's defaults: the page resumes instead of hydrating, the Qwik Loader is a module script, and the preloader adds <link rel="modulepreload"> for the bundles the page's listeners may need.

No service worker. Since Qwik 1.14 the preloader has replaced the prefetching service worker; <ServiceWorkerRegister /> stays only in older apps, to unregister it, and the 1.20 starter has neither it nor a service-worker.ts.

Two routeLoader$s in the route file: the cart summary, read from the cart cookie with Qwik City's cookie API, and the catalog (every product without its description, with the search, category and ?view= product from the URL). The page passes their values to its components as props.

Add to cart and the newsletter are routeAction$s used through <Form>: without JavaScript it posts natively, with it Qwik City submits it with fetch and runs the route loaders again, which updates the header's cart.

The actions validate with the scenario's own functions (readCart, add, validEmail) and return failures with fail(): 404 for an unknown product, 422 for a rejected address, with the scenario's message. There is no zod$ schema.

The cart cookie is set with Qwik City's cookie API, with the same name, value and attributes as the scenario's cartCookie(). Its value is live within the request, so the loaders that run after the action read the new cart.

Search and category filters work in the browser: the query (bound with bind:value) and the category are signals, and the list is a useComputed$ over the loader's products, so results change as you type without a request, and without the 200 ms debounce that asking the server would need.

The search form keeps action="/" method="get" and each category is a link to /?category=, so without JavaScript both load the page. With it, preventdefault:submit and preventdefault:click keep the page, and a category's onClick$ sets it and clears the search.
The list is rendered with .map() and a key per product. Each card is a component with primitive props, so a filter change renders only the cards it adds.
The brand link is a plain <a>, a full page load, rather than <Link>: the docs note that full page loads are cheap in Qwik, and the page has no other route.
Quick view asks for the product's details with a server$ function, Qwik City's RPC. Its link's href, ?view=, renders the dialog open on the server without JavaScript.

The <dialog id="quick-view"> opens with showModal() from a useVisibleTask$, the task that runs after rendering, so the modal never shows before its content. The component that holds it only mounts once a product is chosen, so nothing runs eagerly on page load.

Scenario: the shared stylesheet is a plain <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/app.css"> in root.tsx instead of the starter's imported global.css, with no component styles. The only inline <style> is Qwik City's own :root{view-transition-name:none}.
Scenario: plain elements with the reference's src, width, height, loading and decoding, instead of Qwik's image optimization.
The title comes from the route's head export. RouterHead renders it with the viewport meta, without the starter's canonical link and favicon.
The shared modules are imported from ../../scenario. For `npm run dev`, server.fs.allow lets Vite's dev server serve that folder; production builds need no setting.

stacks.name: SvelteKit
stacks.summary: The page rendered per request by SvelteKit's Node adapter and hydrated by Svelte 5. Search and category live in the URL and filter the list in the browser; add to cart and the newsletter are form actions enhanced with use:enhance; the quick view is a shallow-routed modal.

idioms.choice: adapter-node builds a standalone Node server: `vite build`, then `node build`, which reads PORT, HOST and ORIGIN from the environment.

The project is laid out the way `npx sv create` writes it: SvelteKit's options passed to its Vite plugin in vite.config.js (with runes mode on) and the template's src/app.html, with adapter-node in place of adapter-auto.
A `$scenario` alias points at the shared scenario modules outside the app's folder, which the server imports rather than copying; Vite's server.fs.allow lets the dev server read them.

One +page.server.js load returns the cart from the `cart` cookie, the product listing and the quick view's product. It reads only the `view` search parameter: SvelteKit tracks search parameters one by one, so changing the search or the category does not run it again.

Search and category are search parameters in the URL, where the docs keep filters that affect server rendering. Categories are plain links, so choosing one clears the search. The page reads both from page.url and filters the products it already has with $derived, so a filter change is a client-side navigation with no request.

The search box is a GET form, which the router handles like a link. It is sent on every input (requestSubmit) with data-sveltekit-keepfocus, -noscroll and -replacestate, so results update as you type without a history entry per key. Filtering in the browser needs no debounce.

Add to cart and the newsletter are named form actions (?/add and ?/subscribe), so they work without JavaScript. Form actions are the stable API; the form remote function the docs point to as their successor is still experimental.
Both forms use use:enhance with its defaults: it posts with fetch and, after a success, resets the form and re-runs the page's load (invalidateAll), which reads the cart cookie the action set.

The cart cookie is written with SvelteKit's cookies API (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax and Secure by default) in the shared format, and read with cookies.get, which also sees a cookie set earlier in the same request, so a post without JavaScript renders the new cart.
An invalid email returns fail(422) with the message, which the page shows through the form prop, with or without JavaScript.

The quick view uses shallow routing, as the docs show for a modal: the link's click handler awaits preloadData (already started by data-sveltekit-preload-data on hover or tap), then calls pushState, and the dialog opens with showModal(); Back closes it. The link's address, /?view=<id>, is the fallback: the server renders it with the dialog open.
Add to cart inside the quick view calls refreshAll after the action instead of use:enhance's default invalidateAll, which also resets page.state and would close the dialog.
data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover" on <body>, as in the default template: a link's data starts loading when the pointer rests on it or a finger touches it.
The shared stylesheet is a plain <link> in src/app.html, and no component has a <style> block, as the scenario requires.
Images are plain elements with the reference's attributes, as the scenario requires, rather than the @sveltejs/enhanced-img the docs suggest for build-time optimisation.
